title: Cherry Springs State Park, Coudersport, Pennsylvania
seoTitle: Charter Bus to Cherry Springs State Park, Pennsylvania
excerpt: A charter bus to Cherry Springs State Park for stargazing: which viewing field to use, why the moon phase decides your date, and how to plan a night trip.

heroImage.alt: The Milky Way arching over the open viewing field at Cherry Springs State Park

extraImage.alt: Silhouetted stargazers and telescopes on the observation field under a dense star field

body.text: Cherry Springs sits on a 2,300-foot plateau in Potter County with almost nothing around it for miles, which is exactly the point. It was the second place in the world designated an International Dark Sky Park, and on a clear moonless night the Milky Way is bright enough to be genuinely startling. A charter bus to Cherry Springs State Park solves the problem that makes group stargazing hard: getting people to a remote field in the dark and home again safely.
The moon decides your date. Nothing else comes close.

This is the one thing to get right. A full moon washes out the sky as thoroughly as a city would, and a group that travels four hours on the wrong night sees an ordinary sky. Book the trip for the week around a new moon, and treat the date as fixed by astronomy rather than by convenience.

Weather is the second variable and it cannot be planned around, only accepted. If you are bringing a group this far, build in a fallback for the evening — the region has dark-sky lodging and the Pennsylvania Lumber Museum nearby — so a cloudy night is still a trip.
Two fields, and groups want the right one

items: The Night Sky Public Viewing Area: free, open to everybody, and the correct choice for a general group. Open field, no equipment needed, and the place to simply lie back and look up.
The Astronomy Observation Field: for serious observers and astrophotographers, with registration and a fee, stricter light discipline and overnight use.
The park runs public programs and star parties through the season, which are excellent for a group with no astronomy background and are worth checking before you fix a date.

body.text: What your group needs to bring

Warm clothing, considerably more than the daytime forecast suggests. The plateau is cold and damp at night in every season, and a group standing still for two hours in September will feel it. Blankets or reclining chairs make a substantial difference, because looking up while standing is uncomfortable within about ten minutes.

White light is not permitted — red-filtered torches only, and phones need to stay dark or on a red screen setting. Tell the group before you arrive rather than on the field, where one bright screen ruins everybody's night vision for twenty minutes.
Which charter bus suits a night trip

items: Forty to fifty-six: a full-size [charter bus](/fleet/motor-coaches) is the right vehicle for an astronomy club or a school group traveling any distance, with bays for telescopes and chairs and a restroom for a site that has only basic facilities.
Twenty to thirty-two: a [mini bus](/fleet/mini-buses) suits a smaller club and handles the rural approach comfortably.
Ten to fourteen: a [sprinter van](/fleet/sprinter-vans) works for a small group carrying serious equipment.

body.text: The real argument for a charter here is the drive home. Groups leave Cherry Springs somewhere between midnight and three in the morning on unlit rural roads, and having a professional driver rather than a tired volunteer is the whole safety case. Our [event transportation](/services/event-transportation) team schedules night returns as a matter of routine.

The park is about fifteen miles from [Coudersport](/locations/pennsylvania/coudersport), which is the nearest town of any size and where most groups stay or eat beforehand. From [Bradford](/locations/pennsylvania/bradford) it is roughly an hour and a half, from [State College](/locations/pennsylvania/state-college) about two and a half, and from Pittsburgh or Philadelphia four to five.

Groups searching for charter bus rental near me for a stargazing trip should mention the return time in the first conversation. A midnight-to-3am departure is a different booking from a daytime one, and it needs to be priced that way rather than added later.

On a good night the Milky Way runs from horizon to horizon and is bright enough to cast a faint shadow, which almost nobody arriving from a city has seen before. Expect to make out the Andromeda Galaxy with the naked eye, several thousand stars at once rather than the few dozen visible from a suburb, and satellites crossing constantly once your eyes adjust.

Dark adaptation takes about thirty minutes and is destroyed instantly by a single phone screen. Plan for the group to arrive, settle, and then wait — the first twenty minutes are underwhelming and the sky appears to get dramatically better afterwards. It is not the sky changing, it is the eyes.

Summer offers the brightest Milky Way core and the warmest nights. The Perseid meteor shower in mid-August is the single most popular date of the year here, and vehicles and lodging for that week should be booked months rather than weeks ahead.
